e: RDS for SQL Server is a managed service that handles patching, backups, and Multi-AZ failover, reducing operational overhead, and encryption at rest with KMS plus VPC isolation improves security. Self-managed EC2 databases keep the overhead, and S3 or DynamoDB aren't relational SQL Server replacements.

An Auto Scaling group across two Availability Zones behind an ALB provides high availability, and AWS WAF is associated with the ALB (WAF attaches to ALBs, CloudFront, or API Gateway, not Auto Scaling groups or placement groups). Two fixed instances provide less resilience and scaling.

S3 access points, one per application with its own access point policy restricting the prefix, give granular per-application control on a single bucket with little overhead. Per-object ACLs or replicating data to many buckets add large management effort.

Processing each upload with an S3 event to SQS and Lambda (about 150 photos a day, 2 minutes and 512 MB each) is serverless and costs only for actual use. Always-on EC2, ECS, or Elastic Beanstalk resources cost more.

Network Load Balancers support TCP and UDP and can target both EC2 and on-premises IPs, and AWS Global Accelerator with those NLB endpoints improves availability and performance across Regions for TCP and UDP traffic. ALBs and CloudFront handle only HTTP/HTTPS.

A Recycle Bin retention rule for EBS snapshots keeps deleted snapshots recoverable for a set period (such as 7 days) and then permanently removes them, protecting against accidental deletion without keeping snapshots forever and with no development effort. IAM denies would also block the cleanup script, and copies add cost.

A presigned URL gives CloudFormation temporary access to the specific template object in the private bucket for that request, following security best practices. Making the object public, adding an API Gateway front end, or a VPC endpoint doesn't grant that scoped access.

IAM Identity Center gives the external engineers federated, centrally managed console access, and Systems Manager Session Manager provides audited shell access to instances in private subnets without opening SSH ports, bastions, or distributing keys. IAM users and SSH keys are less secure.

A read replica in the same Region offloads the report queries from the primary instance at low cost and with near-real-time data. Cross-Region replicas add transfer cost, the Multi-AZ standby isn't readable, and DMS replication to a new database adds cost and effort.

Detailed monitoring for EC2 publishes CloudWatch metrics at 1-minute granularity (basic is 5 minutes), meeting the 2-minute requirement with no extra infrastructure. The other options use heavy log pipelines that don't provide the metric granularity.

An S3 event notification invoking a Lambda function to create each thumbnail is event-driven and serverless, so for about 150 photos a day it costs almost nothing. Always-on EMR or EC2 are far costlier, and S3 Storage Lens doesn't trigger functions.

Enable S3 Inventory to list the objects and use S3 Batch Operations to invoke a Lambda function that filters out retained objects and deletes the rest, a serverless way to handle millions of objects. EC2 scripts, Batch, or Glue crawlers aren't serverless or suitable.

Giving each Lambda function its own execution role with only the S3 permissions it needs satisfies least privilege and ensures only authorized functions access the data. A shared full-access role is too broad, and Lambda function ARNs aren't valid bucket policy principals (the role ARN is).

S3 with CloudFront serves the static frontend globally and securely, Lambda behind API Gateway removes server management for the microservices, and RDS for MySQL is managed, giving the least operational overhead. EC2-hosted databases or load balancer setups add administration.

ElastiCache for Redis provides in-memory speed, sorted sets suited to leaderboards and rankings, and supports persistence to disk (snapshots/AOF), which Memcached lacks, with little management. S3, CloudFront, or EC2 designs aren't low-latency ranking stores.

Create a separate KMS key per customer so each customer's data is encrypted separately, with granular key policies and CloudTrail logging, using KMS as the centralized managed service. Keys in S3, hardware appliances, or one shared key don't meet the requirements with low overhead.

An ALB with an Auto Scaling group handles traffic growth, SQS durably holds unprocessed orders so none are lost during surges, and RDS Multi-AZ stores processed orders resiliently. NAT gateways, GWLBs, and Redshift aren't suited to order processing.

With millions of tiny (10 KB) files, grouping them into larger objects avoids per-object overhead and minimum-size charges. Glacier Instant Retrieval gives immediate access at low cost for rarely accessed data in year one, then lifecycle to Deep Archive for the cheapest 7-year retention.

A single io1 volume is capped at 64,000 IOPS, so to go beyond that, attach additional io1 volumes and stripe them with LVM (RAID 0) to aggregate IOPS and throughput. Raising IOPS past the volume limit or its size doesn't help, and a storage-optimized instance doesn't change EBS performance.

SNS is the pub/sub service for fan-out to multiple subscribers, and an API Gateway HTTP API is cheaper than a REST API, so HTTP API with Lambda publishing to SNS is the most cost-effective serverless design. SQS queues aren't pub/sub fan-out, and Kinesis with WebSockets costs more.

A larger instance (kept at one instance by an Auto Scaling group of min=max=1 for self-healing) cuts CPU pressure on the single-instance monolith, and an RDS read replica handles the read requests, with the application sending reads to it. Redirecting all writes to a replica isn't possible, and resizing RDS doesn't offload reads.

IAM roles with fine-grained, least-privilege permissions assigned to each developer give secure, auditable, temporary access. Sharing credentials, long-lived access keys, or Cognito user pools (for application users) are insecure or the wrong tool.

Create an AMI of the web server and a launch template, then use an Auto Scaling group with an ALB to scale horizontally, which both resolves the CPU saturation and improves availability. Scaling vertically keeps a single point of failure.

IAM Access Analyzer reviews access across accounts (with an organization zone of trust) and can generate findings and unused-access analysis to identify overly permissive IAM permissions, with little administrative effort. Network Access Analyzer, CloudWatch alarms, and Inspector don't analyze IAM permissions.

S3 Object Lock in compliance mode prevents any user, including the root user, from deleting or overwriting objects during the retention period, satisfying regulatory retention. Governance mode can be bypassed by privileged users, and lifecycle policies or versioning don't prevent deletion.
